flashcards.front: Subject vs object in access control?
flashcards.back_definition: The subject is who or what asks for access (a user, process or service). The object is the resource being protected (a file, table or endpoint).
flashcards.back_example: Subject: user maya. Object: /srv/grades.csv. Action: read.
flashcards.back_confusion: Access control decides which subjects may do which actions on which objects.

flashcards.back_definition: DAC: the owner of a resource decides who gets access. MAC: a central authority assigns labels and clearances that users can't change. RBAC: permissions come from the user's job role.
flashcards.back_example: Linux file permissions are DAC; military SECRET labels are MAC; "all nurses can read charts" is RBAC.
flashcards.back_confusion: No model is best everywhere: MAC is too rigid for most companies, DAC too loose for classified data.
flashcards.back_hook: Owner decides, system decides, role decides.

flashcards.back_definition: A permission is one narrow right (read invoices). A role is a named bundle of permissions given to users together.
flashcards.back_example: Role "Accounts clerk" = read invoices + create invoices.
flashcards.back_confusion: RBAC supports least privilege only if roles are narrow; one huge superuser role defeats it.
flashcards.back_hook: Permissions are bricks; roles are walls.

flashcards.back_definition: Every user, process and service gets only the access it needs to do its job, and nothing more.
flashcards.back_example: The web app's database account can read and insert orders but cannot drop tables.
flashcards.back_confusion: Extra access "just in case" is not harmless: it grows the damage when that account is compromised.
flashcards.back_hook: Need to do, not nice to have.

flashcards.back_definition: Splitting a sensitive process so that no single person or role can complete it alone.
flashcards.back_example: One person creates a supplier; a different person approves payments to it.
flashcards.back_confusion: It prevents both fraud by one insider and mistakes nobody checks.

flashcards.front: How do you counter privilege creep?
flashcards.back_definition: Regular access reviews (recertification), removing access when people change roles, and granting temporary access with an end date.
flashcards.back_example: A quarterly review removes the payroll access a transferred employee kept.
flashcards.back_confusion: Access that was right last year may be wrong today.

flashcards.back_definition: The owner can read, write and execute; the group can read and execute; everyone else has no access. In octal that is 750.
flashcards.back_example: chmod 750 deploy.sh sets exactly these permissions.
flashcards.back_confusion: Execute on a directory means you may enter it, not run it.
flashcards.back_hook: Owner, group, others: 4 read, 2 write, 1 execute.

flashcards.front: Why is a world-writable file or directory dangerous?
flashcards.back_definition: Anyone on the system can change it. If something privileged runs or reads it, any user can escalate their privileges.
flashcards.back_example: A root cron job runs a script in a world-writable folder, so any user can edit the script and get root.
flashcards.back_confusion: Find them with find / -perm -o+w and remove the write bit for others.
flashcards.back_hook: Writable by all, owned by the attacker.

flashcards.front: What is the SUID bit, and why is it risky?
flashcards.back_definition: SUID makes a program run with its owner's privileges, often root, whoever starts it. A flaw in such a program can give a normal user root.
flashcards.back_example: -rwsr-xr-x on /usr/bin/passwd lets users change their own password.
flashcards.back_confusion: Audit SUID files regularly; an unexpected SUID shell or editor is a serious finding.
flashcards.back_hook: The s means it runs as someone else.

flashcards.front: Why shouldn't containers run as root?
flashcards.back_definition: If an attacker escapes a root container, or a host folder is mounted into it, they can act as root on the host.
flashcards.back_example: A container running as root with the host's / mounted can rewrite the host's files.
flashcards.back_confusion: Run containers as a non-root user, drop capabilities and mount only what is needed.
flashcards.back_hook: Root inside can mean root outside.

flashcards.front: How do stolen credentials enable lateral movement?
flashcards.back_definition: The attacker logs into other systems as the victim, often reusing hashes or tickets without knowing the password (pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket).
flashcards.back_example: An admin's hash taken from a workstation logs the attacker into the file server.
flashcards.back_confusion: A strong password alone does not stop hash replay; MFA, credential hygiene and segmentation do more.

flashcards.front: What signs suggest lateral movement in progress?
flashcards.back_definition: One account logging into many hosts it never used before, at odd hours, or running admin tools for the first time.
flashcards.back_example: A helpdesk account suddenly connects to 30 servers over SMB in ten minutes.
flashcards.back_confusion: These behaviour signals can be caught as it happens, not just afterwards.
flashcards.back_hook: One user, too many doors, too fast.

flashcards.front: Name the three states of data.
flashcards.back_definition: At rest (stored), in transit (moving across a network), and in use (being processed in memory).
flashcards.back_example: Disk encryption protects data at rest; TLS protects data in transit.
flashcards.back_confusion: Data in use is the hardest to protect, since it must be decrypted to be processed.
